NONPROFIT TAX-EXEMPT STATUS APPLICATION (FEDERAL AND CALIFORNIA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

NONPROFIT TAX-EXEMPT STATUS APPLICATION — INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE
This information sheet concerns Acme, Inc. and describes, in general terms, the federal and California processes for a nonprofit corporation to obtain recognized tax-exempt status. Several other documents in this library — covering nonprofit public benefit, nonprofit mutual benefit, nonprofit religious, and unincorporated nonprofit association formation — each note that forming a nonprofit entity under California law is a separate question from obtaining tax-exempt recognition, without themselves addressing that separate question. This document is the one those documents point to as unaddressed: it covers (1) the federal organizational and operational requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3), (2) the federal notice requirement of 26 U.S.C. § 508(a) that generally must be satisfied before a new organization is treated as a § 501(c)(3) organization, (3) California's parallel state-law exemption under Revenue and Taxation Code § 23701d, and (4) the two statutory pathways to recognized California exemption set out in Revenue and Taxation Code § 23701(a)-(b). It does not address obtaining an employer identification number, unrelated business income tax, the private-foundation-versus-public-charity classification tests beyond the basic presumption described below, state or local sales and property tax exemptions, or the Attorney General's charitable-trust registration and reporting requirements, each of which is a separate matter this document does not cover. This document is informational only. It does not itself apply for, obtain, or confer tax-exempt status for Acme, Inc. or any other organization under any federal or California statute, and it does not determine whether Acme, Inc. or any other organization meets any statutory requirement described below on its particular facts.

FEDERAL ORGANIZATIONAL AND OPERATIONAL REQUIREMENTS — 26 U.S.C. § 501(C)(3)
Federal tax exemption under 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) is available to a corporation, community chest, fund, or foundation only if it is organized and operated exclusively for one or more of a specific, closed list of purposes named in the statute — religious, charitable, scientific, testing for public safety, literary, or educational purposes, fostering national or international amateur sports competition (subject to a further athletic-facilities-and-equipment limitation), or the prevention of cruelty to children or animals. The same statutory sentence adds three further conditions that apply regardless of which listed purpose an organization pursues: no part of its net earnings may inure to the benefit of any private shareholder or individual; no substantial part of its activities may consist of carrying on propaganda or otherwise attempting to influence legislation, except as otherwise provided in a separate subsection of the same section; and the organization must not participate in, or intervene in, any political campaign on behalf of or in opposition to any candidate for public office. All of these conditions come from the single statutory paragraph defining the § 501(c)(3) category itself, rather than from separate provisions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Corporations, and any community chest, fund, or foundation, organized and operated exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific, testing for public safety, literary, or educational purposes , or to foster national or international amateur sports competition (but only if no part of its activities involve the provision of athletic facilities or equipment), or for the prevention of cruelty to children or animals, no part of the net earnings of which inures to the benefit of any private shareholder or individual, no substantial part of the activities of which is carrying on propaganda, or otherwise attempting, to influence legislation (except as otherwise provided in subsection (h)), and which does not participate in, or intervene in (including the publishing or distributing of statements), any political campaign on behalf of (or in opposition to) any candidate for public office."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3), Internal Revenue Code, the federal charitable/religious/educational tax-exemption category and its inurement, lobbying, and political-campaign conditions (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/501)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) itself, one paragraph within the longer list of exempt-organization categories in § 501(c); it does not restate the Treasury regulations implementing the "organizational test" and "operational test" (already discussed, for the organizational test, in this project's nonprofit_purpose_state_vs_federal clause), which add further detail — for example on how an organization's articles must be worded — beyond what the statutory text itself says. No case law is cited in this clause: before relying on any court decision, this document's preparation included one lightweight CourtListener case-law search to confirm quota availability, and that search returned a 429 rate-limit response indicating the daily quota was already exhausted; rather than wait for the quota to reset, this document proceeds on statutory text alone and discloses that choice here. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any organization's purposes or activities satisfy this statute, which is a determination made by the IRS, not by this document.

FEDERAL NOTICE REQUIREMENT FOR RECOGNITION AND THE PRIVATE-FOUNDATION PRESUMPTION — 26 U.S.C. § 508
A separate section of the Internal Revenue Code, 26 U.S.C. § 508, governs whether and when an organization otherwise meeting § 501(c)(3)'s substantive requirements is actually treated as a § 501(c)(3) organization. Under subsection (a), an organization organized after October 9, 1969 is not treated as described in § 501(c)(3) unless it has given notice to the Secretary, in the manner the Secretary prescribes by regulation, that it is applying for recognition of that status — and if notice is given late, the organization is not treated as a § 501(c)(3) organization for any period before the notice was given. Separately, under subsection (b), any organization described in § 501(c)(3) that does not notify the Secretary that it is not a private foundation is presumed to be a private foundation. Subsection (c) exempts two categories from both of these rules without any notice at all: churches, their integrated auxiliaries, and conventions or associations of churches; and any organization that is not a private foundation and whose gross receipts in each taxable year are normally not more than $5,000.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as provided in subsection (c), an organization organized after October 9, 1969 , shall not be treated as an organization described in section 501(c)(3)"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 508(a), Internal Revenue Code, the notice-of-application requirement for new organizations to be treated as described in § 501(c)(3) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/508)
  "unless it has given notice to the Secretary in such manner as the Secretary may by regulations prescribe, that it is applying for recognition of such status"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 508(a)(1), Internal Revenue Code, the substance of the required notice (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/508)
  "Except as provided in subsection (c), any organization (including an organization in existence on October 9, 1969 ) which is described in section 501(c)(3) and which does not notify the Secretary, at such time and in such manner as the Secretary may by regulations prescribe, that it is not a private foundation shall be presumed to be a private foundation."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 508(b), Internal Revenue Code, the presumption that an organization is a private foundation absent notice otherwise (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/508)
  "any organization which is not a private foundation (as defined in section 509(a)) and the gross receipts of which in each taxable year are normally not more than $5,000."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1), Internal Revenue Code, the church and small-organization exceptions to subsections (a) and (b) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/508)
  Known gap: The statutory text of § 508(a) says only that notice must be given "in such manner as the Secretary may by regulations prescribe" and "within the time prescribed by the Secretary by regulations" — it does not itself name a specific application form or a specific number of months, and this clause does not restate the separate Treasury regulations that fill in those details, which this document did not independently verify against a fetched regulatory source. No case law is cited in this clause for the same quota-exhaustion reason disclosed in this document's federal-organizational-test clause. This document is informational only: it does not itself give notice to the IRS on behalf of any organization and does not determine whether any organization has satisfied this section's notice requirement or fits within either exception in subsection (c).

CALIFORNIA'S PARALLEL ORGANIZATIONAL AND OPERATIONAL TEST — REV. & TAX. CODE § 23701D
California's own state-law exemption for the kind of organization that would qualify federally under § 501(c)(3) is codified as a separate numbered statute, Revenue and Taxation Code § 23701d — note that, in California's own numbering convention, the letter is appended directly to the section number with no parenthesis or period between them, rather than being written as a lettered subdivision of a single "§ 23701." Section 23701d(a) tracks the federal purposes list closely: a corporation, community chest, or trust organized and operated exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific, testing-for-public-safety, literary, or educational purposes (with the same amateur-sports and cruelty-prevention categories and the same no-inurement, limited-lobbying, and no-political-campaign conditions found in the federal statute). California's statute goes further than the bare text of the federal one, however: § 23701d(a) itself spells out an "irrevocable dedication of assets" requirement, stating in the statutory text that an organization is not organized exclusively for exempt purposes unless its assets are irrevocably dedicated to those purposes, meaning that on dissolution or on the impossibility of carrying out its specific purposes, the assets must continue to be devoted to exempt purposes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A corporation, community chest or trust, organized and operated exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific, testing for public safety, literary, or educational purposes, or to foster national or international amateur sports competition (but only if no part of its activities involved the provision of athletic facilities or equipment), or for the prevention of cruelty to children or animals, no part of the net earnings of which inures to the benefit of any private shareholder or individual, no substantial part of the activities of which is carrying on propaganda or otherwise attempting to influence legislation (except as otherwise provided in Section 23704.5), and which does not participate in, or intervene in (including the publishing or distribution of statements), any political campaign on behalf of (or in opposition to) any candidate for public office."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23701d(a), California's own charitable/religious/educational tax-exemption category, paralleling 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23701d.)
  "An organization is not organized exclusively for exempt purposes listed above unless its assets are irrevocably dedicated to one or more purposes listed in this section. Dedication of assets requires that in the event of dissolution of an organization or the impossibility of performing the specific organizational purposes the assets would continue to be devoted to exempt purposes."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23701d(a), California's own statutory irrevocable-dedication-of-assets requirement, written directly into the exemption statute itself (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23701d.)
  Known gap: This corrects an assumption worth stating plainly: the requirement that an organization's assets be irrevocably dedicated to exempt purposes on dissolution is written directly into the text of California's own statute, Rev. & Tax. Code § 23701d(a); the equivalent federal requirement is not found in the text of 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) itself, but rather in the Treasury regulations implementing it. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of that one state's own parallel exemption category and its added dedication-of-assets language, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. No case law is cited here for the same CourtListener quota-exhaustion reason disclosed elsewhere in this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any organization's articles or activities satisfy this section, which is a determination made by the Franchise Tax Board, not by this document.

CALIFORNIA'S TWO STATUTORY PATHWAYS TO RECOGNIZED STATE EXEMPTION — REV. & TAX. CODE § 23701(A)-(B)
Revenue and Taxation Code § 23701 — the general section governing all of the lettered exemption categories that follow it, including § 23701d — sets out two different statutory routes to recognized state exemption. Under subdivision (a), an organization is exempt only if an application for exemption is submitted in the form prescribed by the Franchise Tax Board and the Franchise Tax Board issues a determination exempting the organization from tax. Under subdivision (b), however, an organization organized and operated for nonprofit purposes under any of several listed sections — including § 23701d — is exempt upon its submission to the Franchise Tax Board of either a copy of the determination letter or ruling issued by the Internal Revenue Service recognizing the organization's federal tax exemption under specified Internal Revenue Code categories, or a copy of a group exemption letter covering the organization as a subordinate. Upon receipt of either document, the statute requires the Franchise Tax Board to issue an acknowledgment that the organization is exempt, rather than a full determination — a materially different, IRS-determination-dependent process from the general application-and-determination route in subdivision (a).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An application for exemption is submitted in the form prescribed by the Franchise Tax Board."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23701(a), California's general application-and-determination pathway to state exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23701.)
  "The Franchise Tax Board issues a determination exempting the organization from tax."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23701(a)(2), California's general pathway, the required Franchise Tax Board determination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23701.)
  "an organization organized and operated for nonprofit purposes in accordance with Section 23701a, 23701d, 23701e, 23701f, 23701g, or 23701w shall be exempt from taxes imposed by this part, except as provided in this article or in Article 2 (commencing with Section 23731), upon its submission to the Franchise Tax Board of one of the following"
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23701(b)(1), California's alternate pathway for organizations, including those under § 23701d, that already hold IRS recognition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23701.)
  "A copy of the determination letter or ruling issued by the Internal Revenue Service recognizing the organization’s exemption from federal income tax under Section 501(a) of the Internal Revenue Code, as an organization described in Section 501(c)(3), (c)(4), (c)(5), (c)(6), (c)(7), or (c)(19) of the Internal Revenue Code."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23701(b)(1)(A), California's alternate pathway, the IRS determination letter document that may be submitted instead of a separate state application (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23701.)
  "Upon receipt of the documents required in subparagraph (A) or (B) of paragraph (1), the Franchise Tax Board shall issue an acknowledgment that the organization is exempt from taxes imposed by this part, except as provided in this article or in Article 2 (commencing with Section 23731)."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23701(b)(2)(A), California's alternate pathway, the Franchise Tax Board's resulting acknowledgment rather than a full determination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23701.)
  Known gap: This section's text does not itself name any specific form number, such as the numbers commonly used to refer to the Franchise Tax Board's general exemption application and its shorter counterpart for organizations that already hold IRS documentation; this document did not independently verify current form numbers, form-revision dates, or filing fees against the Franchise Tax Board's own website, which returned an access-denied response (HTTP 403) when checked while preparing this document, so no specific current fee or form-revision date is stated anywhere in this document. This is one state's statute, describing that one state's own application framework, not a claim about which state's procedures govern a specific corporation. No case law is cited here for the same CourtListener quota-exhaustion reason disclosed elsewhere in this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself submit any application or determination-letter copy to the Franchise Tax Board and does not determine which of the two pathways is available to any particular organization.

PROCEDURAL DETAILS THIS DOCUMENT DOES NOT STATE
Neither the federal statutes nor the California statutes described in this document name specific application form numbers, specific dollar filing-fee amounts, or specific form-revision dates; those details are set administratively by the IRS and by the Franchise Tax Board, and this document does not restate them because they change from time to time and could not be verified, at the time this document was prepared, against a current, independently-fetched Franchise Tax Board web page (which returned an access-denied response) and were only partially checkable against the IRS's own published guidance rather than against statutory or regulatory text itself. What the statutes described above do establish is the structure of the choice involved: a new organization seeking § 501(c)(3) recognition must satisfy 26 U.S.C. § 508(a)'s notice requirement in whatever manner and timeframe the Secretary's regulations prescribe, and an organization that has already obtained an IRS determination letter or ruling recognizing its federal exemption may submit a copy of that document to the Franchise Tax Board under Rev. & Tax. Code § 23701(b)(1)(A), rather than proceeding through the separate general application-and-determination process in § 23701(a), to obtain California's parallel state exemption. Current form numbers, current fee schedules, and current filing procedures for either the federal or the state process are not stated anywhere in this document.
